{
  "plain_name": "Wrongly encoded signature accepted",
  "weakness": "When it reads an ECDSA signature in DER form, the affected code does not check that the top bit of the first byte is zero for each of the signature's two numbers, r and s. As a result it accepts signature bytes that the fixed version refuses, so the same signature is accepted in more than one byte form (the advisory calls this signature malleability).",
  "weakness_quote": {"source": "S1", "text": "In the Elliptic package 6.5.6 for Node.js, ECDSA signature malleability occurs because there is a missing check for whether the leading bit of r and s is zero."},
  "kind": "accepts_bad_signature",
  "area": "ecdsa_signature_check",
  "affected": {"versions": ">= 2.0.0, <= 6.5.6 (the record gives introduced 2.0.0 and last known affected version range <= 6.5.6)", "quote": {"source": "S1", "text": "\"last_known_affected_version_range\": \"<= 6.5.6\""}},
  "fixed": {"version": "6.5.7", "quote": {"source": "S1", "text": "\"fixed\": \"6.5.7\""}},
  "notes": "The advisory's sentence names only 6.5.6, but the same record gives a range: S1 also has the line \"introduced\": \"2.0.0\", so the versions listed as affected run from 2.0.0 up to and including 6.5.6. The excerpts show code for 6.5.6 and 6.5.7 only, so the start at 2.0.0 rests on the record alone. The missing check is about the top bit of the first byte of r and of s, not about r or s being the number zero. The difference shown is only in the function that reads DER-encoded signatures (_importDER): 6.5.7 adds the line if ((data[p.place] & 128) !== 0) { followed by return false, once for r and once for s; 6.5.6 has neither, and the \"Leading zeroes\" check is the same in both. What the sources show is 6.5.6 accepting a second byte form of the same r and s (the number written without a zero byte in front, so that its first byte has the top bit set); they do not show a signature being accepted for a message it was not made for."
}
